title: The Two Thieves (Español)
summary: Two burglars rob a merchant's vault, then try to cheat each other out of the loot. Birbal uses their mutual distrust to recover the treasure. [ES]
full_text:
Two cunning burglars, Kallu and Ballu, broke into a wealthy moneylender's mansion in Agra and escaped with a heavy iron chest containing five thousand gold mohurs. Hiding in a ruined mausoleum outside the city walls, they sat down to divide the loot.

Kallu said: 'I am hungry after our hard work. You guard the gold here, while I run to the village bazaar to buy roasted meat and sweet bread.'

As Kallu walked to the village, greed seized his heart: 'Why should I share half this fortune with Ballu? If I buy rat poison and mix it into his bread, he will die, and the entire five thousand gold coins will belong to me alone!'

Kallu bought the food, poisoned Ballu's share, and hurried back.

Meanwhile, sitting in the tomb, Ballu was thinking identical thoughts: 'Why should I share half the gold with Kallu? When he returns with the food, I will sneak behind him, strike him with this heavy stone, bury his body, and keep the entire treasure for myself!'

When Kallu returned and stepped into the dark chamber holding the bread, Ballu leaped from the shadows and crushed Kallu's skull with the heavy rock, killing him instantly!

Ballu laughed triumphantly: 'The gold is mine! All mine!'

Hungry and exhausted, Ballu sat down on the bloodstained floor and ravenously ate the sweet bread that Kallu had brought.

Within twenty minutes, the violent poison gripped his stomach. Howling in agony, Ballu collapsed across his partner's dead body and perished in the dust!

The next morning, Birbal and the city watch discovered the two corpses and the untouched iron chest.

Presenting the recovered gold to Emperor Akbar, Birbal remarked with grave irony:

'Sire, behold the fruit of unrighteous gain. The dishonest believe they can cheat the moral laws of creation. But evil carries the seeds of its own destruction; in plotting against each other, the two thieves executed justice upon themselves without needing an imperial executioner.'

Akbar ordered the gold restored to the merchant, marvelling at how divine justice operates in the shadows.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Two Thieves"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
quiz.hint: Consider the virtues praised in world folklore.

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace
quiz.hint: Reflect upon the resolution of the story.

discussion_questions.prompt: What is the main situation at the beginning of "The Two Thieves"?
Why does this story teach that "Wit beats power"?
How could you use this lesson in your own school or family life?
Was the character’s final decision fair and kind to everyone?
Imagine an alternate peaceful ending or a new creative adventure for these characters.

reflection_prompt: Have you ever had to choose between acting quickly in anger or waiting patiently to understand the truth?
